n: Chapter 3 shifts to one suffering man speaking for his people. It is a triple acrostic: every three verses begin with the same Hebrew letter. He has felt the “rod” of God’s discipline.

f.g: A shepherd’s or father’s rod, a symbol of discipline; Isaiah calls Assyria “the rod of mine anger.”

n: Instead of guiding him into light like a shepherd, God seems to have led him into darkness. The man feels his life has been turned upside down.
He feels God’s hand turned against him over and over, all day long—an honest description of how affliction can feel.

f.w: he turneth his hand against me

n: Grief has aged his body and broken his bones—physical images for deep inner pain.
Like an army building siege works around a city, God has surrounded him with bitterness and hardship.

f.g: A bitter, poisonous herb; a symbol of bitterness.

n: He feels as if he were buried among those who died long ago, forgotten in darkness.

f.w: as they that be dead of old

n: Walled in and weighed down with chains, he cannot escape—the experience of a prisoner and of a besieged city.
Even his loud prayers seem to go unheard. Scripture does not hide that faithful people sometimes feel heaven is closed.
His road is blocked with cut stone and his paths are twisted; every route forward seems shut.

f.g: Carefully cut building stone—a solid, deliberate wall.

n: God feels like a bear or lion waiting in ambush—dangerous and unpredictable from the sufferer’s point of view.

f.w: as a bear lying in wait

n: He has been dragged off the path and torn apart, left alone and ruined.
God is pictured as an archer, and the sufferer as the target.

f.w: set me as a mark for the arrow

n: The arrows strike deep into his innermost being.

f.g: Kidneys; in Hebrew thought, the seat of the deepest emotions.

n: His own people laugh at him and make him the subject of their mocking songs—an experience Jeremiah knew personally.

f.w: I was a derision to all my people

n: He has been forced to swallow bitterness until he feels drunk with it.

f.g: A very bitter plant; a symbol of sorrow and judgment.

n: As if made to chew gravel and lie in ashes, he feels humiliated and broken.

f.g: Associated with mourning and deep humiliation.

n: Peace feels far away; he has forgotten what good times were like.
At his lowest point he concludes that his strength and hope from the Lord are gone. The poem honestly records despair before turning toward hope.

f.w: My strength and my hope is perished from the LORD

n: He asks God to remember his misery—the bitter “wormwood and gall” of his suffering.
He keeps remembering his pain, and it weighs his soul down.
The great turning point of the book. He chooses to call something else to mind, and that choice brings hope.

f.w: This I recall to my mind

n: What he remembers is the Lord’s steadfast love: it is only because of God’s mercies that his people are not completely destroyed, for his compassion never fails.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed—loyal, covenant love that holds on.

n: God’s mercies are “new every morning”—a fresh supply each day. “Great is thy faithfulness” has become one of the most beloved lines in scripture and hymnody.
Like the priestly tribe of Levi, which received no land because the Lord was their inheritance, he declares that the Lord himself is his portion and hope.
The Lord is good to those who patiently wait for him and seek him.

f.g: To wait in Hebrew (qavah) carries the sense of hopeful expectation.

n: It is good to hope and wait quietly for the Lord to save—faith that does not demand an immediate answer.
It is good to learn to bear a yoke while young. Trials accepted early can shape strong, humble disciples.
The wise sufferer sits alone in silence, accepting the burden God has allowed rather than raging against it.
Putting one’s face in the dust was a gesture of total humility; he humbles himself in case there may still be hope.

f.w: putteth his mouth in the dust

n: He offers his cheek to the one who strikes him and accepts insult. This anticipates the Savior’s teaching and his own patient suffering.

f.w: He giveth his cheek to him that smiteth him

n: The reason for hope: the Lord does not reject forever.

f.w: the Lord will not cast off for ever

n: Even when he allows grief, he will show compassion because his mercies are abundant.
A tender insight into God’s character: he does not afflict people “from his heart” or take pleasure in their pain. Discipline is not his delight.
Verses 34–36 form one sentence: God does not approve of crushing prisoners underfoot…

f.g: Captives and the helpless—exactly what exiled Judah had become.

n: …or of denying someone justice right in front of the Most High…
…or of cheating a person in a lawsuit. The Lord sees and disapproves of all such injustice.

f.g: To twist or pervert (a legal case).

n: Nothing happens unless the Lord allows it. Babylon’s victory was not outside his control.

f.w: Who is he that saith, and it cometh to pass

n: Both blessing and calamity come within God’s sovereign rule. The Hebrew “evil” here means disaster, not moral wickedness.
Why should a living person complain about suffering that came because of his own sins? Being alive at all is a mercy.
The poem now invites the whole community: let us examine our lives and come back to the Lord. This is the heart of repentance.

f.w: Let us search and try our ways

n: Lift not only hands but hearts to God—outward prayer joined to inward sincerity.

f.w: lift up our heart with our hands

n: A frank confession: we sinned and rebelled, and you have not (yet) forgiven.

f.w: We have transgressed and have rebelled

n: The people describe God’s anger as wrapping around them and chasing them down without pity.
God seems hidden behind a cloud so prayers cannot get through—the feeling of distance that sin creates.

f.w: that our prayer should not pass through

n: Israel has become like trash and scrapings among the nations. Paul later uses similar words for how the world treated the apostles.
Enemies open their mouths wide to mock. (This begins a new letter group, matching 2:16.)
Terror, traps, ruin, and destruction have come on them—a string of sound-alike Hebrew words.

f.g: In Hebrew paḥad wa-paḥat, a wordplay; compare Isaiah 24:17.

n: The speaker’s eyes run with rivers of tears for his ruined people—very like Jeremiah’s own laments.

f.w: Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water

n: His tears flow without stopping…
…until the Lord looks down from heaven and sees. Persistent prayer waits for God’s attention.

f.w: look down, and behold from heaven

n: What he sees of the suffering young women of the city grieves his heart.
Enemies hunted him like a bird for no reason—an echo of Jeremiah’s persecution by his own people.
They threw him into a pit to die and sealed it with a stone—strikingly like Jeremiah’s imprisonment in a muddy cistern.

f.g: Hebrew bor, a pit or cistern.

n: Water rose over his head; he thought, “I’m finished.” Floodwaters are a common biblical picture of overwhelming danger.
From the bottom of the pit he called on the Lord’s name.
Now he speaks with confidence: you heard my voice. He asks God not to close his ear to his gasping cry.

f.g: My gasping or sighing—a prayer too weak for words.

n: “You came near when I called; you said, ‘Fear not.’” Personal experience of God’s nearness anchors his hope.
The Lord has acted as his defense lawyer and his redeemer. Latter-day Saints see in this the role of Jesus Christ as Advocate and Redeemer.

f.w: thou hast pleaded the causes of my soul

n: He asks the Lord, who has seen the wrong done to him, to judge his case.
God has seen all the enemies’ revenge and schemes.
The Lord has also heard their insults and plots.
He has heard what his enemies say and plan all day long.
Whether they sit or stand, they sing mocking songs about him.
He asks the Lord to repay his enemies according to their deeds—leaving vengeance to God rather than taking it himself.

f.w: according to the work of their hands

n: He prays that God will give them hardness of heart and his curse.

f.g: Possibly “hardness” or a “covering” of heart; the Hebrew word is rare.

n: The chapter ends with a plea for God to pursue and destroy the oppressors. Such prayers leave justice in God’s hands; the Savior later taught his followers to pray even for enemies.

f.w: Persecute and destroy them in anger
